summary:
John Bercow (born 1963) was Conservative MP for Buckingham from 1997 to 2019 and Speaker of the House of Commons from 2009 to 2019. He left the Conservatives on becoming Speaker, was re-elected unopposed in 2010, 2015 and 2017, and became the first postwar Speaker elected four times. After leaving Parliament, he joined Labour in 2021; the party suspended him in 2022 after upholding 21 complaints that he had bullied staff.

Bercow grew up in north London, earned a first-class degree in government from Essex, and was a councillor in Lambeth from 1986 to 1990. Once a right-wing Conservative activist, he served in opposition front-bench roles under Iain Duncan Smith and Michael Howard, but his views shifted. He resigned from the front bench in 2002 rather than oppose adoption by unmarried couples, then returned and was dismissed in 2004. Before becoming Speaker, he reviewed support for children with speech and language needs, leading the government to pledge £52 million.

As Speaker, Bercow oversaw the Commons through four prime ministers and became known for his forceful management of debates. He supported LGBT equality and charities, but faced criticism over his expenses, including claims related to his homes and travel. He was appointed Chancellor of the University of Bedfordshire in 2014 and the University of Essex in 2017, and became a part-time politics professor at Royal Holloway in 2020. Since Betty Boothroyd’s death in 2023, he has been the only living former Commons Speaker.
